title: Pins
objectives: Define a pin: a piece that can't or shouldn't move because doing so exposes a more valuable piece behind it
Distinguish an absolute pin (illegal to move, king behind) from a relative pin (legal but costly, valuable piece behind)
Create a pin along a diagonal and along a rank
Recognize that a pinned piece's 'defense' of a nearby square is often not real

steps.text: A pin happens when a piece sits between an attacker and something more valuable behind it, on the same line. Here, the bishop on b5 pins the knight on c6 to the king on e8 — the diagonal runs straight through all three. The knight can't legally move at all: doing so would expose its own king to check, and that's illegal. This is an absolute pin.

steps.prompt: A pinned piece can always still move — it's just usually a bad idea.

feedback.default: That's only true for a relative pin, where a valuable piece (not the king) sits behind. When the king itself is behind the pinned piece, moving it is illegal, not just unwise — the rules of chess don't allow you to expose your own king to check.

steps.successExplanation: Right to flag this as false in general — an absolute pin (king behind) makes the move illegal, not just a bad idea. A relative pin (any other piece behind) is legal but usually costly.

steps.prompt: A bishop pins a knight to the black queen — not the king. The knight is worth about 3 points, the queen about 9. What kind of pin is this, and can the knight legally move?
options: An absolute pin — the knight can't legally move
A relative pin — the knight can legally move, but moving it loses the queen
Not a pin at all, since the king isn't involved

feedback.default: Only a pin against the king makes the move illegal. Pinning a piece to any other, more valuable piece is still a real pin — a relative pin — but the pinned piece can legally move; it's just a bad trade to do so.

steps.successExplanation: Right — a relative pin doesn't make the move illegal, but moving the pinned piece hands over the more valuable piece behind it.

steps.prompt: Move the bishop onto the diagonal that pins the knight to the king.

hints.text: Find the diagonal that passes through both the knight and the king.
The knight and king both sit on this diagonal.
Bc6 pins the knight on d7 to the king on e8 — the knight can no longer legally move at all.

feedback.default: That doesn't create a pin. Find the diagonal square where the bishop's line runs straight through the knight and then the king.

steps.successExplanation: Bc6 pins the knight to the king along the c6-d7-e8 diagonal. Once pinned this way, the knight has zero legal moves — any knight move takes it off a diagonal line, which would expose the king.

steps.prompt: The rook on d5 is pinned to the king and can't recapture. Capture the pawn it's supposedly defending.

hints.text: The rook on d5 can't move off the d-file without exposing its own king — so does it really defend the pawn next to it?
Your bishop's diagonal reaches the pawn directly.
Bxe5 wins the pawn for free. Recapturing on e5 would take the rook off the d-file, exposing the king — an absolutely pinned piece can't defend anything off its own line.

feedback.default: That doesn't win the pawn cleanly. Remember: the rook is pinned to its own king along the d-file, so check whether it can actually recapture here.

steps.successExplanation: Bxe5 wins the pawn for free. The rook on d5 is absolutely pinned to the king along the d-file — if it recaptured on e5, it would move off the file and expose the king to your rook. A pinned piece's 'defense' often isn't real.

steps.prompt: Move the rook onto the rank where it pins the enemy rook to the king.

hints.text: Pins aren't only diagonal — a rook can pin along a rank, too. Find the rank both the enemy rook and king share.
The enemy rook and king both sit on this rank.
Ra5 pins the rook on e5 to the king on h5 along the 5th rank. A rook pinned like this has no legal moves at all — it can't slide off the rank, and it can't move diagonally in the first place.

feedback.default: That doesn't create a pin. Find the rank the enemy king and rook already share, and put your rook on it.

steps.successExplanation: Ra5 pins the rook to the king along the 5th rank. A pin doesn't have to be diagonal — a rook, and especially a queen, pin just as effectively along ranks and files.

steps.prompt: A rook is absolutely pinned along a file to its own king by your rook. Which squares can the pinned rook still legally move to?
options: Any square on the board — pins don't restrict where a piece can go
Only squares still on that same file — moving off it would be illegal
It has no legal moves at all
Only one square, chosen at random

feedback.default: A rook pinned along a file can still slide up and down that exact file (including capturing the pinning piece, if reachable) — what it can't do is leave the file, since that would expose the king.

steps.successExplanation: Right — a rook pinned along a file can still move along that same file. It's only moves that would take it off the pinning line that are illegal.

steps.summary: A pin happens when a piece sits between an attacker and something more valuable behind it. If the king is behind, moving the pinned piece is illegal — an absolute pin. If any other, more valuable piece is behind, moving is legal but costly — a relative pin. Either way, a pinned piece's apparent 'defense' of a nearby square often isn't real, since it may not be able to legally recapture at all.
